title: Dia duit! Saying hello
intro: Irish says hello with a blessing. Someone wishes God on you, you hand back God and Mary.
It sounds holy. In practice it is about as pious as 'cheers, mate'.

words.note: Many speakers make the D almost a J: JEE-uh gwitch.

words.english: Hello back (God and Mary to you)
words.note: The reply goes one better than the greeting. Plenty of people just say 'Dia duit' back.
The textbook form. Connacht also says 'Cén chaoi a bhfuil tú?', Ulster 'Cad é mar atá tú?'
To more than one person: go raibh maith agaibh (ug-iv).
Céad míle fáilte: a hundred thousand welcomes.
Leaving? Say slán agat to whoever stays. Staying? Say slán leat to whoever goes.

tip: Irish has three main dialects: Connacht, Munster and Ulster. Our sound guides follow Connacht, spoken here in Galway and Connemara; where Munster or Ulster differ, the card says so.

title: A haon, a dó: numbers, and no word for yes
intro: Out here we count boats, birds and days till the ferry runs again.
And here's a thing: Irish has no single word for yes or no. Ask me something and I'll show you.

words.note: When counting aloud, each number takes 'a' in front. The h keeps two vowels from colliding.
Six to nine: a sé, a seacht, a hocht, a naoi. The ch is the soft breathy sound in German 'ich'.
Answers 'An bhfuil...?' (Is...? Are...?). 'An bhfuil tú tuirseach?' Are you tired? 'Tá.' I am.
The no to the same question. Other verbs work the same way: you answer with the verb you were asked.

tip: No yes, no no: Irish answers a question by repeating its verb, yes or not. It's why Irish people speaking English often answer 'I am' or 'I do' instead of plain 'yes'.

title: Aimsir: weather and the wild
intro: Connemara does four seasons before lunch. You'll want the words for all of them.
Mountain, sea, tree: learn those and half the map starts making sense.

words.note: Said with real feeling, because it doesn't come often.
The final ch is the throaty sound in 'loch'.
Hides in English maps as Slieve: Slieve Donard in the Mournes is Sliabh Dónairt.
Connacht and Munster say it to rhyme with 'crown'; Ulster keeps it closer to 'krann'.

tip: Weather in Irish is something that is, not something that happens: 'Tá sé fliuch', it is wet. The same 'Tá' you met as a yes.

title: Sláinte! Tea, pints and the pub
intro: Welcome to Kerry, where the Irish is Munster Irish and the tea is strong enough to stand a spoon in.
Order in Irish and nobody minds a wobble. Order in a hurry and everybody does.

words.note: Reply: sláinte mhaith (SLAWN-cheh WAH), good health.
Pionta, le do thoil: a pint, please.
The most useful two words in any pub.
Uisce beatha, 'water of life', is where the English word whiskey comes from.
Here in Munster the stress jumps to the long vowel: uh-RAWN.

tip: Munster Irish often stresses a long vowel later in the word, where Connacht and Ulster stress the first syllable. Same spelling, different music.

title: Bally, Kil, Dun: reading the map
intro: Most place names in Ireland are Irish in an English coat. Take the coat off and they tell you what's there.
A town, a church, a fort, an island, a glen, a lake, a rock. That covers a lot of the country.

words.note: Ballycastle on the Antrim coast is Baile an Chaistil, town of the castle.
Kilkenny is Cill Chainnigh, the church of Cainneach, the saint called Canice in English.
Donegal is Dún na nGall, the fort of the foreigners.
Enniskillen is Inis Ceithleann, Ceithleann's island, on the River Erne between its two loughs.
Glenveagh in Donegal is Gleann Bheatha. Ulster says it closer to 'glan'.
Lough Neagh, the biggest lake in these isles, is Loch nEathach.
The Carrick in Carrick-a-Rede, the rope bridge on the Antrim coast.
As in Ardnacrusha by Limerick, home of the Shannon hydro scheme.

tip: Scottish Gaelic shares many of these (baile, gleann, loch), because the two languages are close cousins. Cousins, not twins: the spelling and the sounds differ.

title: Séimhiú: the h that changes everything
intro: Welcome to the Coláiste. Every summer, teenagers from all over Ireland come to places like this to live through Irish.
Today: séimhiú, lenition. Put an h after the first letter and the sound goes soft. Watch.

words.note: 'Mo' (my) lenites: c becomes ch, the throaty sound in 'loch'.
mh sounds like w here in Connacht and in Ulster; Munster says v.
'An' (the) lenites feminine nouns like bean. Masculine ones stay put: an fear, the man.
Calling someone by name lenites it. Sh sounds like h: Dia duit, a Sheáin!

tip: Only b, c, d, f, g, m, p, s and t take the h. bh and mh go v or w, ch is throaty, sh and th go h, and fh goes silent. Welsh and Scottish Gaelic mutate too, each in its own way.
